one_sentence_story: In 1972–1975 at the University of Toronto, Fergus Craik, Robert Lockhart, and Endel Tulving proved that repeating words mechanically barely touches long-term memory — whereas half a second of deep semantic questioning triples to quintuples retention (~17% to ~80%+) even when you aren't trying to memorize.
so_what_for_you: Throw away passive yellow highlighters: as Daniel Willingham puts it from Craik & Lockhart's law, *'Memory is the residue of thought'* — ask one 'Why?' or 'What is a real example?' question per paragraph so left prefrontal and hippocampal circuits bind it automatically.

jargon_map.plain: principle that memory strength depends on how deeply an item's meaning is analyzed rather than how long it sits in short-term rehearsal
jargon_map.analogy: carving a word deep into oak (meaning) vs tracing your finger on water (shallow font)

jargon_map.term: shallow vs phonemic vs deep encoding
jargon_map.plain: checking surface print ('CAPITAL LETTERS?' ~17% recall) vs sound ('rhymes with crate?' ~48%) vs conceptual fit ('fits in a sentence?' ~82%)
jargon_map.analogy: inspecting a book's font vs reading its title aloud vs debating its plot

jargon_map.term: Type I maintenance vs Type II elaborative rehearsal
jargon_map.plain: repeating a phone number mechanically to keep it from fading vs linking new facts to existing knowledge
jargon_map.analogy: juggling balls in place vs snapping Lego bricks onto a castle

jargon_map.plain: finding that deep semantic questions WITHOUT any warning of a quiz beat deliberate 'try hard to memorize!' shallow studying
jargon_map.analogy: proof there is no willpower 'Save' button — only how you think

jargon_map.analogy: packing snow boots for snow and swim fins for the reef
